claim: Two waves of transcriptional activation occur in chicken embryos, one shortly after fertilization and another at Eyal-Giladi and Kochav Stage V.
source: We established that two waves of transcriptional activation occurred, one shortly after fertilisation and another at Eyal-Giladi and Kochav Stage V.
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of pre-mRNA expression and differential expression analysis showing upregulated pre-mRNAs between oocyte and zygote (1st wave) and between EGK.III and EGK.VI (2nd wave).

claim: 1544 single nucleotide polymorphisms across 424 transcripts derived from parents were expressed in offspring during early embryonic stages.
source: We found 1544 single nucleotide polymorphisms across 424 transcripts derived from parents that were expressed in offspring during the early embryonic stages.
evidence: Supported by whole-genome sequencing of parents and whole-transcriptome sequencing of hybrid embryos, with breed-specific SNP identification.

claim: Only the maternal genome is activated in the chicken zygote during the first wave of transcriptional activation.
source: Surprisingly, only the maternal genome was activated in the zygote, and the paternal genome remained silent until the second-wave, regardless of the presence of a paternal pronucleus or supernumerary sperm in the egg.
evidence: Supported by allelic expression analysis showing all transcripts identified in the zygote stage exhibited maternally derived expression, validated by Sanger sequencing of six pre-mRNAs.

claim: The paternal genome remains silent until the second wave of transcriptional activation.
source: Surprisingly, only the maternal genome was activated in the zygote, and the paternal genome remained silent until the second-wave, regardless of the presence of a paternal pronucleus or supernumerary sperm in the egg.
evidence: Supported by allelic expression analysis showing no paternal alleles in zygote transcripts, with bi-allelic expression appearing only at EGK.X stage.

claim: Maternal genes activated during the first wave are involved in cleavage and are replaced by bi-allelic expression.
source: The identified maternal genes involved in cleavage that were replaced by bi-allelic expression.
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis showing 1st wave-activated maternal transcripts enriched in cell cycle, Notch signaling, Wnt signaling pathways, and observation that most maternally derived transcripts converted to bi-allelic expression after MZT at EGK.X.

claim: The timing and mechanisms of zygotic genome activation have been investigated in various species.
source: The timing and mechanisms of ZGA have been investigated in various species (Aanes et al., 2011; Baugh et al., 2003; Harvey et al., 2013; Karr et al., 1985; Lee et al., 2013b; Leichsenring et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2008; Newport and Kirschner, 1982; Poccia et al., 1985; Tan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies on ZGA in various species.

claim: In mammals, the first wave of transcriptional activation occurs after fertilization during pronucleus formation.
source: In mammals, the first wave (1st wave) of transcriptional activation (also known as minor ZGA) occurs after fertilisation, during pronucleus (PN) formation.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about mammalian ZGA timing.

claim: The second wave of transcriptional activation in mammals occurs during the two-cell stage in mice and the eight-cell stage in humans.
source: The subsequent second wave (2nd wave) of transcriptional activation (major ZGA) occurs during the two-cell stage of mice and the eight-cell stage of humans (Aoki et al., 1997; Braude et al., 1988; Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on mammalian ZGA timing.

claim: Gene activation during early cell cleavage has been described in chicken and quail embryos.
source: In avian species, reports in chicken and quail embryos have described gene activation during early cell cleavage (Nagai et al., 2015; Olszańska et al., 1984), but transcriptional activation has not been investigated during fertilisation.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on avian gene activation.

claim: Transcriptional activation has not been investigated during fertilization in avian species prior to this study.
source: In avian species, reports in chicken and quail embryos have described gene activation during early cell cleavage (Nagai et al., 2015; Olszańska et al., 1984), but transcriptional activation has not been investigated during fertilisation.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature showing gap in knowledge.

claim: In mice, transcription from the paternal pronucleus is greater than that from the maternal pronucleus during the first wave of ZGA.
source: In mice, the most distinctive feature of the 1st wave in the PN stage is that transcription from the paternal PN is greater than that from the maternal PN, due to the epigenetic regulation of the latter (Aoki et al., 1997; Aoshima et al., 2015; Bouniol et al., 1995; Wu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on mouse ZGA.

claim: The first wave of ZGA in mice is highly promiscuous, with expression of untranslatable mRNAs and intergenic regions.
source: In addition, the 1st wave is highly promiscuous, in that the expression of untranslatable mRNAs and intergenic regions is observed (Abe et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on mouse ZGA characteristics.

claim: In zebrafish, the mitochondrial genome is activated in the one-cell embryo.
source: In zebrafish, the mitochondrial genome is activated in the one-cell embryo (Heyn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on zebrafish ZGA.

claim: In plants, the zygotic genome is activated soon after fertilization.
source: In plants, the zygotic genome is activated soon after fertilisation, and rice zygotes show asymmetric activation of parental genomes (Anderson et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on plant ZGA.

claim: Rice zygotes show asymmetric activation of parental genomes.
source: In plants, the zygotic genome is activated soon after fertilisation, and rice zygotes show asymmetric activation of parental genomes (Anderson et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on rice ZGA.

claim: The earliest expressed genes in ZGA are species-specific.
source: As the earliest expressed genes in ZGA are species-specific (Heyn et al., 2014), the patterns of transcription during the 1st wave should be examined so that we can understand early embryogenesis in each species.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study and logical inference about need for species-specific investigation.

claim: Polyspermy is a distinctive feature in birds.
source: As polyspermy is a distinctive feature in birds (Snook et al., 2011; Iwao, 2012), we hypothesised that the 1st wave derived from the parental genome would exhibit unique characteristics.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on avian fertilization.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of pre-mRNA expression shows that zygotes differ from oocytes.
source: Hierarchical clustering of precursor mRNA (pre-mRNA) expression demonstrated that zygotes differed from oocytes, suggesting dynamic changes in primary transcripts after fertilisation (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Phosphorylated RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain first appears during late EGK.II to early EGK.III.
source: Phosphorylated RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain first appeared during the late EGK.II to early EGK.III (Nagai et al., 2015), but the expression of pre-mRNA differed between EGK.III and EGK.VI (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study and comparison with pre-mRNA expression data.

claim: The expression of pre-mRNA differs between EGK.III and EGK.VI.
source: Phosphorylated RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain first appeared during the late EGK.II to early EGK.III (Nagai et al., 2015), but the expression of pre-mRNA differed between EGK.III and EGK.VI (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of upregulated pre-mRNAs in the zygote compared to the oocyte provides evidence of a first wave of transcriptional activation.
source: The number of upregulated pre-mRNAs that are found in the zygote when compared to the oocyte provides evidence of a 1st wave (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A large number of pre-mRNAs are upregulated between EGK.III and EGK.VI, revealing the presence of a second wave.
source: In addition, a large number of pre-mRNAs were upregulated between EGK.III and EGK.VI, revealing the presence of a 2nd wave.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of pre-mRNAs.

claim: The number of expressed regions is reduced during EGK.I and EGK.III but increases after EGK.VI.
source: The number of expressed regions was reduced during EGK.I and EGK.III but increased after EGK.VI.
evidence: Supported by quantification of expressed genomic regions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of expressed intronic regions decreases after fertilization and increases gradually after EGK.VI.
source: Of all of the genomic regions that are expressed, the proportion of expressed intronic regions decreased after fertilisation and increased gradually after EGK.VI (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of intronic read distribution shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The proportion of expressed intergenic regions is constant regardless of transcriptional activation in chickens.
source: Unlike the expression patterns seen during the minor ZGA in mammals (Abe et al., 2015), the proportion of expressed intergenic regions was constant regardless of transcriptional activation, indicating no expression of these regions during the 1st wave in chickens.
evidence: Supported by analysis of intergenic region expression shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and comparison with mammalian data.

claim: Large numbers of up- and downregulated mRNAs and lincRNAs are observed during the first wave.
source: In genic regions, large numbers of up- and downregulated mRNAs and long intergenic noncoding RNAs (lincRNAs) were observed during the 1st wave, while other RNAs were mostly downregulated after fertilisation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting a potential role for long transcripts in the early cleavage stages.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Other RNA types besides mRNAs and lincRNAs are mostly downregulated after fertilization.
source: In genic regions, large numbers of up- and downregulated mRNAs and long intergenic noncoding RNAs (lincRNAs) were observed during the 1st wave, while other RNAs were mostly downregulated after fertilisation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting a potential role for long transcripts in the early cleavage stages.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Long transcripts may have a potential role in early cleavage stages.
source: In genic regions, large numbers of up- and downregulated mRNAs and long intergenic noncoding RNAs (lincRNAs) were observed during the 1st wave, while other RNAs were mostly downregulated after fertilisation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting a potential role for long transcripts in the early cleavage stages.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that long transcripts (mRNAs and lincRNAs) are specifically upregulated during the 1st wave.

claim: All RNA types are significantly upregulated during the second wave.
source: All RNA types were significantly upregulated during the 2nd wave.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: DLX6, GATA2, ZIC4, LYPD2, IFITM5, and NKX6-3 are upregulated during the first wave of transcriptional activation.
source: Six upregulated genes in each wave were selected as representative genes (Supplementary file 1): DLX6, GATA2, ZIC4, LYPD2, IFITM5 and NKX6-3 for the 1st wave, and WNT11, WNT3A, C8ORF22, NAT8L, PCOLCE2 and AKAP2 for the 2nd wave.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR validation shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: WNT11, WNT3A, C8ORF22, NAT8L, PCOLCE2, and AKAP2 are upregulated during the second wave of transcriptional activation.
source: Six upregulated genes in each wave were selected as representative genes (Supplementary file 1): DLX6, GATA2, ZIC4, LYPD2, IFITM5 and NKX6-3 for the 1st wave, and WNT11, WNT3A, C8ORF22, NAT8L, PCOLCE2 and AKAP2 for the 2nd wave.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR validation shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The second wave of transcriptional activation in chicken occurs between EGK.IV and EGK.V, not between EGK.II and EGK.III.
source: The validated genes belonging to the 2nd wave of activation indicated a lack of transcriptional activity during rapid cellularisation in the cleavage period, and showed that the 2nd wave of transcriptional activation in chicken occurred not between EGK.II and EGK.III, but between EGK.IV and EGK.V.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR validation of 2nd wave genes showing no expression until EGK.IV-V.

claim: There is a lack of transcriptional activity during rapid cellularization in the cleavage period.
source: The validated genes belonging to the 2nd wave of activation indicated a lack of transcriptional activity during rapid cellularisation in the cleavage period, and showed that the 2nd wave of transcriptional activation in chicken occurred not between EGK.II and EGK.III, but between EGK.IV and EGK.V.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 2nd wave genes are not expressed during early cleavage stages (EGK.II-III).

claim: A total of 1544 parentally derived SNPs were detected, distributed across 424 transcripts including mRNAs and lincRNAs.
source: A total of 1544 parentally derived SNPs were detected, distributed across 424 transcripts including mRNAs and lincRNAs (Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome sequencing of parents and whole-transcriptome sequencing of hybrid embryos with breed-specific SNP identification.

claim: All transcripts identified in the zygote stage exhibit maternally derived expression during the first wave.
source: Interestingly, all of the transcripts that were identified in the zygote stage exhibited maternally derived expression during the 1st wave (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: Supported by allelic expression analysis of breed-specific SNPs in hybrid embryos.

claim: Most maternally derived transcripts are replaced by bi-allelic expression at the EGK.X stage, except for seven mRNAs and two lincRNAs.
source: Most of the maternally derived transcripts, except for seven mRNAs and two lincRNAs, were replaced as bi-allelic expression occurred in the EGK.X stage.
evidence: Supported by allelic expression analysis showing conversion from maternal-only to bi-allelic expression.

claim: Nine transcripts that remain maternally expressed at EGK.X could be interpreted as residual maternal transcripts not activated during the second wave, rather than genomic-imprinted genes.
source: These nine transcripts could be interpreted as residual maternal transcripts that were not activated during the 2nd wave, rather than as genomic-imprinted genes, which are not conserved in avian species (Frésard et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that genomic imprinting is not conserved in avian species, supported by citation.

claim: Genomic-imprinted genes are not conserved in avian species.
source: These nine transcripts could be interpreted as residual maternal transcripts that were not activated during the 2nd wave, rather than as genomic-imprinted genes, which are not conserved in avian species (Frésard et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on avian genomic imprinting.

claim: MAP7D1, ESCO1, CCNB3, SYTL1, GRHL1, and LLGL1 show maternal allelic expression in the zygote until the EGK.VI stage, except for GRHL1.
source: All of the selected genes showed maternal allelic expression in the zygote until the EGK.VI stage, except for the GRHL1 gene.
evidence: Supported by Sanger sequencing validation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Maternally derived genes convert to bi-allelic expression after the maternal-to-zygotic transition at EGK.X.
source: These maternally derived genes converted to bi-allelic expression after the maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT) at EGK.X.
evidence: Supported by Sanger sequencing validation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The chicken first wave phenomenon is distinguished from mammals, where transcriptional activity in the paternal pronucleus is two times greater than in the maternal pronucleus.
source: This phenomenon is distinguished from that in mammals, in which transcriptional activity in the paternal PN is two times greater than that in the maternal PN (Aoki et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on comparison of chicken data showing maternal-only expression with cited mammalian data showing paternal-dominant expression.

claim: There is no possibility that activated transcripts are derived from supernumerary sperm nuclei and paternal pronucleus in chickens.
source: These results indicate that there is no possibility that the activated transcripts are derived from the supernumerary sperm nuclei and paternal PN, in contrast to the data from mammals (Aoki et al., 1997; Bouniol et al., 1995).
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that all zygote transcripts are maternally derived, with no paternal contribution.

claim: First wave-activated maternal transcripts are enriched in cell cycle, Notch signaling pathway, Wnt signaling pathway, regulation of transcription DNA-templated, and regulation of small GTPase-mediated signal transduction pathways.
source: The analysis revealed that the 1st wave-activated maternal transcripts were enriched in the following pathways: cell cycle; Notch signalling pathway; Wnt signalling pathway; regulation of transcription, DNA-templated; and regulation of small GTPase-mediated signal transduction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pathways activated from the maternal genome are involved in rapid asymmetric cellularization during the cleavage period in chickens.
source: These pathways were activated from the maternal genome and are involved in rapid asymmetric cellularisation during the cleavage period in chickens (Hwang et al., 2018c) and other species (Castanon et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2015; Priess, 2005; Tse et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis and citations to studies on cell division pathways.

claim: The first wave in mice promotes low-level expression of numerous non-functional genes.
source: While the 1st wave in mice promotes the low-level expression of numerous non-functional genes (Abe et al., 2015), the maternal genes activated during the 1st wave in chickens seem to be related to early cell division in embryogenesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on mouse ZGA characteristics.

claim: Maternal genes activated during the first wave in chickens are related to early cell division in embryogenesis.
source: While the 1st wave in mice promotes the low-level expression of numerous non-functional genes (Abe et al., 2015), the maternal genes activated during the 1st wave in chickens seem to be related to early cell division in embryogenesis.
evidence: Based on inference from functional enrichment analysis showing enrichment in cell cycle and related pathways.

claim: The characteristics of the first wave of ZGA vary among species.
source: As demonstrated in previous studies, the characteristics of the 1st wave vary among species (Abe et al., 2015; Anderson et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Heyn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing different ZGA characteristics in different species.

claim: After maternal-to-zygotic transition, most expressed genes are derived from both paternal and maternal genomes.
source: However, after MZT, most expressed genes were derived from both paternal and maternal genomes.
evidence: Supported by allelic expression analysis showing bi-allelic expression at EGK.X stage.

claim: Transcripts affected by the first wave are functionally involved in asymmetric rapid cellularization and fundamental regulation of further development.
source: Functionally, transcripts affected by the 1st wave were involved in asymmetric rapid cellularisation and in the fundamental regulation of further development (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on functional enrichment analysis and schematic summary in Figure 4C.

claim: Polyspermic animals require a number of sperm to activate large eggs.
source: Polyspermic animals require a number of sperm to activate large eggs (Iwao, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on polyspermy.

claim: Polyspermic embryos of sea urchin demonstrate that transcriptional activation after fertilization is greatly stimulated by the pronucleus of supernumerary sperm.
source: In addition to pathological mitosis (Snook et al., 2011), polyspermic embryos of sea urchin demonstrated that transcriptional activation after fertilisation was greatly stimulated by the PN of supernumerary sperm (Poccia et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on sea urchin polyspermy.

claim: Disproportionate genome contribution in polyspermic embryos could result in an excessive amount of transcription.
source: Such a disproportionate genome contribution could result in an excessive amount of transcription.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the observation that multiple sperm contribute genetic material.

claim: The total polyspermy number varies and is positively correlated with egg size.
source: The total polyspermy number reportedly varies (Hemmings and Birkhead, 2015; Lee et al., 2013a) and is positively correlated with egg size (Birkhead et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on polyspermy variation and correlation with egg size.

claim: Individual sperm provide genomic diversity but could result in genomic instability if different types of transcripts are expressed by various sperm nuclei.
source: Individual sperm provide genomic diversity (Wang et al., 2012) but could result in genomic instability if different types of transcripts are expressed by various sperm nuclei.
evidence: Based on inference from cited study on sperm genomic diversity and logical reasoning about potential consequences.

claim: Polyspermic animals may have evolved means of inhibiting the activation of the paternal pronucleus to control gene expression levels from the first wave.
source: Therefore, polyspermic animals may have evolved means of inhibiting the activation of the paternal PN to control gene expression levels from the 1st wave.
evidence: Based on speculation from the observation of maternal-only expression in chicken zygotes and reasoning about evolutionary pressures in polyspermic species.

claim: The maternally derived first wave is essential for early development and evolutionary outcomes in avian species.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the maternally derived 1st wave is essential for early development and evolutionary outcomes in avian species.
evidence: Based on inference from the functional enrichment analysis showing involvement in cell cycle and development pathways, and speculation about evolutionary significance.

claim: Each embryo contained an average of 2.1 µg of total RNA.
source: Each embryo contained an average of 2.1 µg of total RNA (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA quantification measurements from collected embryos.

claim: A total of 4275 differentially expressed mRNAs were detected between oocyte and zygote stages.
source: A total of 4275 differentially expressed mRNAs were detected (Figure 3C; FDR-adjusted p<0.05), among which 1883 were upregulated and 2392 were downregulated in the zygote stage compared to the oocyte.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of single embryonic WTS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 1883 mRNAs are upregulated and 2392 are downregulated in the zygote stage compared to the oocyte.
source: A total of 4275 differentially expressed mRNAs were detected (Figure 3C; FDR-adjusted p<0.05), among which 1883 were upregulated and 2392 were downregulated in the zygote stage compared to the oocyte.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of single embryonic WTS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 118 lincRNAs are upregulated and 786 are downregulated in the zygote stage compared to the oocyte.
source: We also observed that 118 and 786 lincRNAs were up- and downregulated, respectively.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of single embryonic WTS data.

claim: 10,298 mRNAs and 2,507 lincRNAs are differentially expressed between zygote and EGK.X stages.
source: Owing to the dramatic changes in early development between fertilisation and oviposition, 10,298 mRNAs and 2507 lincRNAs were differentially expressed between the zygote and EGK.X stages (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of single embryonic WTS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A large number of primary transcripts are upregulated in the zygote stage compared to the oocyte stage.
source: We also observed a large number of primary transcripts that are upregulated in the zygote stage when compared to the oocyte stage(Supplementary file 2B; FDR-adjusted p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of pre-mRNAs from single embryonic WTS data.

claim: Primary transcriptional activation occurs as developmental stage moves from oocytes to zygotes at single-embryo resolution.
source: These results once again demonstrate that primary transcriptional activation occurs as developmental stage moves from oocytes to zygotes at single-embryo resolution, in terms of the numbers of differentially expressed pre-mRNAs and long transcripts.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of pre-mRNAs and long transcripts from single embryonic WTS data.

claim: WTS samples generated from single embryos cluster according to their respective stages.
source: The WTS samples generated from the single embryos were clustered according to their respective stages (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by multidimensional scaling plot shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Zygote, EGK.I, and EGK.III have similar transcriptome profiles.
source: Zygote, EGK.I and EGK.III had similar transcriptome profiles.
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In total, 8.38 billion reads or approximately 2.53 Gbp of sequences were generated from whole-genome sequencing.
source: In total, 8.38 billion reads or ~2.53 Gbp of sequences were generated.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data from WGS of six parental chickens.

claim: The average alignment rate for WGS reads to the reference genome was 91.61%.
source: Using Bowtie 2 (v2.2.5) (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012), reads were aligned to the reference genome sequence galGal4 (Build v 4.82) with an average alignment rate of 91.61%.
evidence: Supported by alignment statistics from WGS data analysis.

claim: 10,529,469 variants were detected from whole-genome sequencing, of which 9,805,997 variants (93.129%) were previously known variants.
source: As a result, 10,529,469 variants were detected, of which 9,805,997 variants (93.129%) were previously known variants (Supplementary file 5A, B).
evidence: Supported by variant calling analysis from WGS data.

claim: 265,788 variants were detected from RNA-Seq data, of which 248,030 variants (93.319%) were previously known sites.
source: At the end of this process, 265,788 variants were detected, of which 248,030 variants (93.319%) were previously known sites (Supplementary file 5C, D).
evidence: Supported by variant calling analysis from RNA-Seq data.

claim: 216,003 SNPs were identified as breed-specific SNPs.
source: As a result, 216,003 SNPs were identified as breed-specific SNPs.
evidence: Supported by comparison of parental genotypes from WGS data.

claim: 14,817 SNPs were commonly identified in breed-specific SNPs and those derived from RNA-Seq data.
source: After that, two SNP datasets (breed-specific SNPs and their offspring genotypes derived from the RNA-Seq data) were combined to detect maternally and paternally expressed genes, and 14,817 SNPs were commonly identified in breed-specific SNPs and those derived from RNA-Seq data.
evidence: Supported by intersection of SNP datasets from WGS and RNA-Seq.

claim: After filtering steps, 5,666 SNPs remained as parental expression markers.
source: The remaining 5,666 SNPs were annotated using the SnpSift tool with galGal4 and ALDB GTFs.
evidence: Supported by filtering and annotation of SNPs for allelic expression analysis.

claim: 1,544 SNPs were detected as parental expression markers, all of which showed a maternal expression pattern.
source: At the end of this process, 1,544 SNPs were detected as parental expression markers, all of which showed a maternal expression pattern (Supplementary file 5E).
evidence: Supported by final filtering and annotation of SNPs for allelic expression analysis.

claim: Pre-ovulatory and post-ovulatory oocytes show small transcriptomic differences.
source: Owing to the small transcriptomic differences between pre- and post-ovulatory oocytes observed in the previous study (Elis et al., 2008) and the infeasibility of simultaneous acquisition of post-ovulatory oocytes and zygotes from a single hen, only the pre-ovulatory large F1 oocyte was isolated.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on oocyte transcriptomics.

claim: Detection of de novo transcription after fertilization is difficult because of the large number of mRNAs being processed in the oocyte.
source: Detection of de novo transcription after fertilisation is difficult because of the large number of mRNAs that are being processed in the oocyte.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about the challenges of detecting new transcription in the presence of maternal mRNAs.
